metadata.note: The Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific Railroad's own core mainlines, researched from Wikipedia and railroad-history sites in response to a question about whether 'the Rock Island' was depicted on this map -- previously only its Chicago-Joliet commuter stub (see data/metra.geojson's Rock Island District) and a Texas subsidiary it half-owned (see data/burlington_rock_island.geojson) were represented, not its own famous long-distance network. Covers the original 1852-1869 Chicago-Omaha mainline (the 'Rock Island Line' of the folk song, first railroad to bridge the Mississippi and the first to reach the transcontinental connection point at Council Bluffs, one day after the golden spike); the Golden State Route to Los Angeles (jointly run with the Southern Pacific from 1902); and the Rocky Mountain Rocket streamliner to Denver and Colorado Springs (1939-1966), shown as two features sharing a Chicago-Limon trunk since the train split in two at Limon. All predate any GTFS/live-data era and have no modern segment -- the Rock Island entered its third and final bankruptcy in 1975, was ordered liquidated in Jan 1980, and ceased all operations Mar 31 1980, though most of its principal routes survive today under other railroads. Route geometry follows the real intermediate towns each railroad's own history describes, but is a simplified handful of waypoints, not surveyed track centerline. Era boundaries follow real corporate-history milestones (line openings, named-train launches and discontinuations); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not sourced from real timetables. UPDATED: the Golden State Route's geometry (previously 9 sparse hand-placed waypoints) has been real-traced from OpenStreetMap active-rail geometry for the Chicago-Joliet-Kansas City-Liberal, KS-Dalhart, TX-Tucumcari, NM-El Paso stretch (the Rock Island's own trackage), and the El Paso-Los Angeles stretch reuses the already-real-traced geometry from southern_pacific_sunset_route.geojson (the same physical Southern Pacific track both trains used). No gaps needed a straight-line fallback -- this corridor traced cleanly end to end despite the Rock Island's 1980 breakup, since its route was mostly absorbed intact by successor freight operators rather than abandoned. [Update: Rocky Mountain Rocket and Chicago-Omaha geometry refined 20260818 using real OSM/Overpass track data (Iowa Interstate Railroad for Chicago-Omaha via Iowa; abandoned Chicago Rock Island & Pacific-tagged remnants for Omaha-Hastings NE; Union Pacific's Limon Subdivision and the old CRI&P-tagged grade for the Limon-Denver and Limon-Colorado Springs branches). No OSM trace survives for roughly Hastings NE to Limon CO or the final approach into Colorado Springs -- those short stretches are still straight-line interpolation through real intermediate towns (McCook, NE), not surveyed track. The Golden State Route geometry is unchanged from the original waypoint-based version.]
metadata.source: Wikipedia, american-rails.com, trains.com, splives.org, denversrailroads.com, okhistory.org (see conversation for citations)
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

properties.line: Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific: Rocky Mountain Rocket
properties.speed_source: estimated/blended across the line's history; unsourced

segments.note: Construction crews camped at Limon, CO in 1888 building the line on toward Colorado Springs (reaching it that year, connecting with the Colorado Midland); Limon's own depot opened in 1889, the same year the Rock Island struck a trackage deal with the Union Pacific for the final stretch from Limon into Denver. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:
Wikipedia, american-rails.com, trains.com, splives.org, denversrailroads.com, okhistory.org (see conversation for citati…

segments.note: The Rock Island began through Chicago-Colorado service via Omaha Aug 16 1891, running over its original transcontinental-connector mainline as far as Omaha, a new Omaha-Lincoln extension built in 1890 (trading trackage rights to the Union Pacific for use of UP's Missouri River bridge at Council Bluffs-Omaha), and its own new line west of Lincoln from there. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:
Wikipedia, american-rails.com, trains.com, splives.org, denversrailroads.com, okhistory.org (see conversation for citati…

segments.note: Fairbury, NE's grand Renaissance Revival depot opened Feb 10 1914, a fitting stop for the road's flagship Chicago-Denver train, the heavyweight, 27-hour Rocky Mountain Limited (train numbers 7 and 8), running LaSalle Street Station-Denver Union Station and, in a splitting section, on to Colorado Springs. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:
Wikipedia, american-rails.com, trains.com, splives.org, denversrailroads.com, okhistory.org (see conversation for citati…

segments.note: The Burlington's Pioneer Zephyr kicked off the streamliner era with its record Denver-Chicago 'Dawn-to-Dusk' dash (13h05m) in 1934; by 1936 the Burlington's Denver Zephyr and Union Pacific's City of Denver had both settled into a regular 16-hour schedule. The cash-strapped, bankrupt Rock Island answered by fielding six new streamlined 'Rocket' trainsets in 1936, then bought two more specifically for its Chicago-Denver train. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:
Wikipedia, american-rails.com, trains.com, splives.org, denversrailroads.com, okhistory.org (see conversation for citati…

segments.note: The streamlined Rocky Mountain Rocket entered service Nov 12 1939 on a 20-hour Chicago-Denver schedule -- slower than its rivals but still profitable. Its original consist ran reserved reclining-seat coaches, a diner with a cocktail lounge, a 10-section/4-roomette sleeper (Denver-Chicago), and a trailing buffet-sleeper-lounge observation car with 5 double bedrooms, competing against Union Pacific's City of Denver, the Missouri Pacific's Colorado Eagle, and the Burlington's Denver Zephyr. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:
Wikipedia, american-rails.com, trains.com, splives.org, denversrailroads.com, okhistory.org (see conversation for citati…

segments.note: Facing hard competition from airlines and the new interstate highways, the Rocky Mountain Rocket lost its sleeping and dining cars in July 1965, replaced by simple snack cars, as the Rock Island's finances kept crumbling. It made its last run Oct 16 1966, five years before Amtrak. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
